article_sentences: The Andhra Pradesh Eastern Power Distribution Company Limited (APEPDCL) has stepped up its preparedness for Cyclone Arnab and is concentrating on Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema, Godavari and Kakinada districts, towards which the storm is expected to make landfall.

Following the India Meteorological Department (IMD)’s warning about Cyclone Arnab over the east-central and adjoining south-east Bay of Bengal, the utility has mobilised personnel, machinery and electrical materials to minimise disruptions and speed up power restoration in affected areas.
APEPDCL has opened 30 divisional control rooms, in addition to 11 circle-level control rooms, to monitor the situation and coordinate emergency response.
Kakinada and East Godavari have three divisional control rooms each, and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema has two.
A separate cell has been established at the corporate office to coordinate manpower deployment round the clock under the supervision of the Chief General Manager (Operations and Customer Service).
APEPDCL CMD I. Prudhvi Tej held a teleconference with senior engineering officials to review cyclone preparedness.
The utility has also sought 150 teams of 10 personnel each from the Southern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Limited (APSPDCL) and requested additional materials from it.
The utility has arranged 394 contractor teams comprising 4,056 personnel for emergency response and restoration work.
The available resources include 211 diesel generator sets, 273 pole-drilling machines, 517 power saws and 318 earth movers and cranes.
A fleet of 366 departmental and private vehicles has been listed to transport personnel and materials to affected locations.
Another 100 mobile handsets have been arranged for communication during emergency operations.
APEPDCL said it had stocks of conductors, cables, distribution transformers and electric poles as of October 25.

stories.headline: DAC clears proposals worth Rs 2.12 lakh crore for armed forces procurement
stories.title: DAC clears proposals worth Rs 2.12 lakh crore for armed forces procurement
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 26: The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), chaired by Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh on October 26, 2026, accorded Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) i.e. in-principle administrative to various capital acquisition proposals of the Defence Forces at an estimated cost of about Rs 2,12,000 crore. For the Indian Army, approval was accorded for the procurement of High Mobility Vehicles (HMV), Self-Propelled Tracked Gun System, Gun Shot Response System (GSRS), Light Multi Role Helicopters (LMRH), Very Short-Range Air Defence System (VSHORADS), Platform Based Counter Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS), Unmanned Aerial System Brick Long Range, Surveillance UAV, Integrated Surveillance and Strike System and Long Range Kamikaze Drone System. The HMVs will enhance operational capabilities, logistic support and mobility in challenging terrains. The Self-Propelled Tracked Gun System will provide matching mobility and firepower to mechanised formations. The GSRS will serve as a force multiplier providing real-time situational awareness of the forces. The LMRH will be used by both the Indian Army and the Indian Air Force for Reconnaissance and Surveillance, Combat, Search and Rescue of troops, Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief etc. The VSHORADS will engage new generation small size aerial threats, while C-UAS will enhance survivability of Tanks in the modern battlefield. The Surveillance and Drone Systems will enhance the surveillance and targeting capabilities of the Indian Army. For the Indian Navy, approval was given for the procurement of Active Offboard Decoy System (AODS) and other major Naval platforms. The AODS will enhance the credibility of anti-missiles defence, especially against modern anti-ship missiles of adversaries. The indigenously designed and constructed major Naval platforms will possess modern-day warfare capabilities and enhance the combat capability of the Navy. For the Indian Air Force, approval was accorded for the procurement of Helicopters, Air Defence Systems, Weapons and Mobile X-Band Doppler Weather Radar System to enhance the air defence and war fighting capabilities. The procurement of Special Utility Helicopters will help the Indian Air Force to meet the important air transport requirements. The X-Band Doppler Weather Radar System will provide high-resolution, localised weather surveillance in forward areas. Out of the total AoNs accorded, approximately 82% of the procurements will be made from the Indian Industry.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Monday agreed to examine a petition challenging the special intensive revision (SIR) of Maharashtra’s electoral rolls, following concerns that voters temporarily displaced by redevelopment projects had been excluded.
A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notices to the Centre, the Election Commission of India and other respondents.
The matter will be heard next on 5 November.
The petition was filed by Arun Anandagiri, a chartered accountant and journalist.
Appearing for him, senior advocate.

Arvind Datar told the court that voters who had temporarily moved out of their homes during redevelopment in Mumbai and Pune were being categorised as “person not found” and removed from the draft rolls.
Datar submitted that around two crore of Maharashtra’s nearly 9.79 crore voters had been excluded.
He also claimed that another 1.22 crore electors had been struck off under the category of “logical discrepancies”.

stories.headline: Pak Army chief and top officials from Makkah pact countries to meet Iranian security czar in Tehran
stories.title: Pak Army chief and top officials from Makkah pact countries to meet Iranian security czar in Tehran
stories.summary: Islamabad, Oct 26: Pakistan Army Chief Asim Munir, Saudi Arabia's defence minister and Turkish intelligence chief are expected to jointly meet top Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday to discuss the regional security situation, according to officials. In separate statements, Pakistan, Saudi and Iranian authorities confirmed the meeting, amid fears that escalating tensions in the region could draw more countries into the fighting. The meeting also comes amid raging tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis in recent weeks, with the Iran-backed group claiming attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and military sites. Saudi Arabia has reported intercepting missiles and drones targeting the kingdom. Field Marshal Munir is visiting Tehran on an "official visit," the Pakistan Army said in a brief statement, without giving details of the trip. This is his second trip to Tehran within a week, amid indications that the US might be preparing for another round of fighting with Iran. Hours earlier, the Iranian Supreme National Security Council's Deputy Secretary Ali Bagheri said that "senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkiye will travel to Tehran as part of efforts to implement the idea of endogenous security in West Asia,” according to the state-run IRNA news agency. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye are part of the Makkah Joint Defence agreement signed in August. According to the pact, any attack on one of the three countries would be treated as an attack against all. The high-level meeting comes days after the Pakistan Army chief met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei in Tehran. Bagheri told state TV that among the visiting dignitaries would be Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin and Pakistan's Army chief Munir. "The purpose of these senior officials’ trip is consultation with Major General Mohsen Rezaei regarding regional security," he said. "All three countries attending this meeting, along with Iran, can take an effective step toward creating endogenous security within the framework of Iran's effective idea for regional security-building with the participation of regional actors, drawing on Iran’s successful experience in national security-building," Bagheri was quoted as saying by IRNA. Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly also confirmed the visit in a post on X, saying that the meetings would be held on Monday. According to him, Minister of Defence Prince Khalid will lead the Saudi delegation during the meeting between Makkah pact countries and Iranian officials. He said the "representatives of Makkah Joint Defence Agreement countries will meet" with Iranian President Pezeshkian and Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Rezaei. Krimly described the visit as “part of the continued efforts by the Makkah Defence Alliance members for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis, and promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions, in support of the mediation efforts carried out by Qatar and Pakistan”. "The visit underscores the pivotal role of Makkah Defence Alliance members in reinforcing regional security and stability, and working with all countries in the region to achieve that goal,” he added. In Tehran, Iran’s Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said that the meeting with officials from the three countries would cover “most pressing issues threatening our region”, which included Israel’s expansionist policies, developments in Palestine and Lebanon. He also said that the topic of “top priority on the agenda would be consequences of the US-Israeli aggression against Iran and its ramifications for the entire region”. The US and Iran signed the Islamabad MoU in June to restore peace in West Asia, advance negotiations on regional security and other contentious issues. The deal ended the conflict that began on February 28 and continued till April 8, when the ceasefire was agreed, followed by talks mediated by Pakistan. Field Marshal Munir and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi have made multiple trips to Tehran as part of Islamabad's efforts to de-escalate tensions in the region. Munir's last visit to Tehran coincided with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's unannounced trip to West Asia. During his meeting with Munir last week, Rezaei told the Pakistani army chief that all enriched nuclear materials will remain in Iran as a national asset, stressing that no negotiations with the US will take place until Washington builds trust by meeting Iran’s conditions, according to the channel. Also, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov last week travelled to Tehran, where he met Iranian leaders and discussed everything from Europe to West Asia, including Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine and Yemen.

The Supreme Court on Monday (October 26) warned that it may order a Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe into alleged illegal mining and the regularisation of mining areas along the Jojari-Luni-Bandi river system in Rajasthan, questioning why State authorities had granted mining leases in areas where illegal mining had been detected, and regularising illegal leases.

A bench of Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Sandeep Mehta cautioned that several officials could face serious consequences if the State failed to take corrective action, while expressing concern over the authorities' failure to protect the rivers despite repeated judicial directions.
“What have you done about providing the statistics of the mining, illegal mining in the rivers?

You have regularized.

That would land many of your officers in hot waters,” Justice Mehta told Additional Solicitor General SV Raju, appearing for Rajasthan.

The Court was hearing the Supreme Court's suo motu proceedings concerning pollution in the Jojari-Luni-Bandi river system, which has affected the environment and the lives of approximately 20 lakh people.

In August, the Court directed that no construction or development activity shall be permitted within 100 metres of the edge of the river system until completion of a scientific exercise to determine and demarcate the High Flood Line and the requisite ecological buffer zones, as an interim measure to protect the river ecosystem from further ecological degradation.

Today, the Court questioned the State's explanation that it had registered hundreds of cases relating to illegal mining, observing that registration of cases did not address the fact that mining areas previously identified as illegal had subsequently been regularised.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court today directed all States/UTs and High Courts to ensure availability of exclusive bar rooms for women lawyers as well as washrooms within their respective jurisdictions.

A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana passed the order, emphasizing that the States/UTs must allocate necessary funds wherever required and the High Courts' building-cum-infrastructure committees must oversee implementation.
"Every State government, Union Territory, and the High Courts are obligated to provide facilities to members of the Bar in terms of directions already issued by this court.

We hasten to add that...it is obligation of all State governments and the High Courts to ensure that wherever in the district courts, sub-divisional (taluka) courts, there are practicing women members in the Bar, irrespective of their strength, however proportionate to such strength, a separate and exclusive women's bar room shall be provided, along with basic amenities like washrooms and other facilities.
With respect thereto, we direct all State governments to allocate the necessary funds, if not already available.
The building-cum-infrastructure committees of the High Courts are directed to take up this issue on priority basis and ensure that all such facilities are created in the district and taluka courts."

Opining that the pattern of basic facilities should be uniform across all states/UTs, the Court called upon the Advocate Generals/Standing Counsels of States/UTs to submit progress reports to the office of Attorney General R Venkataramani so the AG can place a compilation before the court.
It also permitted the petitioners and intervenors to give suggestions to the AG.

Where the suggestions pertain to a particular State, the Court said that the same may be referred by AG Venkataramani to the concerned Advocate General so they may take up the suggestion with the State government for necessary compliance.

During the hearing, AG Venkataramani informed the Court that he had held one meeting with the Advocate Generals and another meeting was proposed to be held by the end of this month to deliberate on the issues.
The CJI impressed upon the parties that the AG shall act as the central nodal authority through whom the states/UTs may furnish their details.
"We would like the Attorney General first to satisfy himself about the facilities, additional allocation of funds and budgets provided by the States" the CJI said.

The matter dates back to 1996, when communal riots in Thoothukudi caused damage to businesses and properties.

However, the State government subsequently issued Government Order G.O.Ms.No.1834, granting uniform compensation of Rs.
2 lakh to all affected persons.
The decision was challenged before the Madras High Court.
Both the Single Judge and the Division Bench favoured compensation in accordance with the recommendations of the one-man commission.
The State government subsequently challenged the High Court's decisions before the Supreme Court.

article_sentences: The plea also challenges the use of Form 6 for voters already enrolled in previous elections.

New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Monday sought the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) response to a plea alleging large-scale deletion of voters from Maharashtra’s electoral rolls during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise, while declining to immediately extend the deadline for filing claims and objections.

A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana issued notice to the ECI on a petition filed by Arun Anandagiri, who alleged that 33% of voters had been deleted from the state’s electoral rolls during the SIR exercise.
The court, however, did not grant the petitioner’s request to extend the deadline on Monday.
The bench said it would consider extending the date if, after hearing the matter, it found that more time was required.
The case is scheduled to be heard next on November 5.
Senior Advocate Arvind Datar, appearing for Anandagiri, raised concerns over voters being left out of the rolls because of changes in their addresses and other details.
He told the court that around 3,500 redevelopment projects were underway in Mumbai and Pune, with old housing societies being demolished and thousands of residents being relocated.

According to the petitioner, such displacement could put voters at risk of losing their names from the electoral rolls if their current address or other details could not be matched during the revision process.
Datar also questioned the use of Form 6 for voters who were already enrolled in previous elections.
He argued that Form 6 is meant for registering new voters and that existing voters should not be required to use the same form to retain their names on the electoral rolls.
The petitioner sought a separate form or process for voters whose names had already appeared on earlier electoral rolls.

article_sentences: There may be a 50 basis points (bps) hike in the repo rate in the Monetary Policy Committee’s December 2026 bi-monthly monetary policy review meeting, according to State Bank of India Chairman CS Setty.
This will be followed by a pause till March-end 2027, he said at a BFSI Summit organised by Business Standard.

The RBI’s rate-setting had upped the policy repo rate by 25 basis points from 5.25 per cent to 5.50 per cent and changed the monetary policy stance from neutral to calibrated tightening at its last meeting (October 5- 7) amid rising inflationary pressures even as growth has been resilient.
Setty observed that increase in interest rates will definitely influence the composition as well as the quantum of credit demand, but not necessarily immediately.
“I think rate-sensitive sectors, particularly the discretionary spending related borrowings probably would moderate.
But I would like to differentiate between weakening credit cycle and moderation in the credit demand.
I think we need to distinguish that.
“One of the important things to recognise is we are entering the rate hike cycle with a robust growth rate — you have a rate hike as well as a projection of 7.1 per cent growth rate.
That means you will have sustained credit growth coming from the real economy’s demand for credit,” he said.
So, if a couple of rate hikes are going to be there, the discretionary consumption demand and consumption credit probably will be impacted.
But it is unlikely that productive activities will see any less demand for credit.
Setty emphasised that there is only so much the interest rates can propel customers to come into deposits.

stories.headline: ISRO’s new chapter: Among resignations, questions remain about future role
stories.title: ISRO’s new chapter: Among resignations, questions remain about future role
stories.summary: Following the successful orbital flight of its flagship rocket in July, Skyroot Aerospace, India’s first space tech unicorn, has already shipped the first stage of its second Vikram-1 vehicle to Sriharikota as preparations for the next mission get under way. It marks an early step towards ambitious national targets because the government is aiming to establish a six-launch-vehicle portfolio and achieve 50 launches a year by 2030. So far, the area was most closely tied to Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro), but now it is the private industry that is expected to play a major role in achieving this target.India is not the only country where national space programmes are slated to remain national while industry is enabled to deliver at scale. “China’s space programme was on par with us till the 2010s. But after that, it was a meteoric rise, thanks to the involvement of the industry in the scaling-up efforts,” says Rohan Ganapathy, CEO and CTO of Bellatrix Aerospace. The Chinese space programme has clocked about 70 space launches already this year.In the United States, Nasa (National Aeronautics and Space Administration), too, has long relied on private industry to deliver the capabilities it needs while retaining control of its missions. For instance, its Commercial Orbital Transportation Services programme, which started in 2006, helped SpaceX and others build cargo vehicles for the International Space Station. The model was later extended to crew transport through the Commercial Crew Programme and to lunar landers and deliveries under the Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative.But even as India opened up the space sector in 2020, with the government stating that the aim is for Isro to hand operational and commercial work to industry and concentrate on research, fears of privatisation have remained. The fears resurfaced in July after over a hundred scientists left for private sector jobs, once again raising the question about the role Isro is expected to play in the coming years.Also Read: Why GSLV-F17 is more than just Isro’s first successful launch of 2026Shifting prioritiesAwais Ahmed, co-founder and CEO of space tech startup Pixxel, says that Isro’s current transition cannot be compared to the handover of Air India to the private sector. In space, he says, what changed is that private firms are now allowed to do what only Isro could do before. “A space research organisation should not face revenue targets or sell satellite capacity, which is why commercial work moved first to Antrix and then to NSIL (the commercial arms of Isro),” he says.Pawan Kumar Chandana, CEO of Skyroot Aerospace, too, says it is different from the private sector taking over Isro. “It is an expansion of India’s space ecosystem,” he says, adding that Isro can concentrate on frontier technologies, human spaceflight, planetary exploration, science missions and high-risk programmes, while industry takes on commercial and repeatable work. Skyroot’s Vikram-1, the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit, benefited from infrastructure and regulation created by Isro, Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe, a single-window autonomous agency under the Department of Space) and the government, he points out. Isro Chairman V Narayanan. Photo by R. Satish Babu / AFPKeyur Gandhi, the director of space regulatory and commercialisation for Dhruva Space, goes a step further. Asked whether Isro needs to adapt, he says, “The answer is no. I think the ecosystem needs to adapt.” Private capacity, he argues, lets Isro move work on operational requirements to other players and use its decades of expertise on next-generation systems, and strategic, scientific and space exploration requirements.An organisation in transitionInside the space agency, the picture appears less settled, according to media reports. The Indian Space Policy 2023 states that Isro will focus primarily on R&D. “Hereafter, mature systems shall be transferred to industries for commercial exploitation. Isro shall focus on R&D in advanced technology, proving newer systems and realisation of space objects for meeting national prerogatives,” the policy states. Agnibaan is a rocket built by Agnikul Cosmos to launch small satellites. Its first test flight took place in May 2024However, on September 4, nine employee associations wrote to Isro Chairman V Narayanan, seeking clarification after IN-SPACe Chairman Pawan Goenka said Isro would eventually stop making launch vehicles, with manufacturing handled by private companies or PSUs. The associations described launch-vehicle work as core competence. They also said that they were not opposed to privatisation as such but wanted clarity on the future relevance of existing staff and centres.On September 7, Narayanan told reporters at the Bengaluru Space Expo that Isro remains a government organisation and is not getting privatised. He noted that it has about 20,000 employees, including more than 8,000 scientists.In a follow-up letter dated October 7, a Joint Action Council representing the nine employee associations acknowledged the chairman’s responses, but stated in a letter that “the core questions regarding the future mandated role of Isro, the policy on privatisation and transfer of manufacturing and operational functions, technology transfer, staffing and recruitment, and employee safeguards remain substantially unanswered”.Compounding the fears of uncertainty, media reports estimate that between 100 and 120 scientists from key space programmes quit over a few months earlier this year. Isro has not published official figures on departures but the Department of Space issued a memorandum dated July 14 tightening rules on voluntary retirement and resignations by scientists.However, some point out that attrition at Isro predates the current debate and is an ongoing concern. According to media reports, in 2023, then Isro chairman S Somanath said about 60 percent of IIT graduates left an Isro recruitment presentation after seeing the salary structure.Gurpeet Singh spent almost eight years in the navigation group at the UR Rao Satellite Centre in Bengaluru, the lead centre for the design, development, and realisation of all satellites within Isro and where most of India’s satellites are built. But he left in July 2025 to join Newton School of Technology as an associate director of academics, and also advises Vyomic, a space startup working on low-Earth-orbit navigation.He believes people often quit Isro because they feel “that mundane, repetitive work is happening at Isro and don’t want to associate with that,” he says. People expect “specialised R&D inside Isro, which is the usual assumption”, he says, adding that, as Isro transfers repetitive tasks, such as end-to-end satellite fabrication, to private companies, that should give its scientists room for deeper research and riskier missions.The second reason, he says, is opportunity in the private sector, which has grown. The third reason is that a number of scientists leave to pursue higher education. “[But] that was always there. That is not a new phenomenon,” he says.Despite the exits, however, he adds that Isro’s size gives it resilience. “It’s such a large organisation, there is huge inertia,” he says. “If one or two people leave, overall momentum is not much affected.” Hiring is still open and young engineers still want to join, he says, and the gap is “manageable”. Bharatiya Antariksh Station is Isro’s planned five-module space station, with the first module due by 2028 and completion by 2035The support ISRO providesIt is not just engineers who want continued association with Isro. Founders, too, describe continuing reliance on Isro’s infrastructure and supply chain. Suyash Singh, CEO of GalaxEye, says Isro’s decades of in-house building has left India with a downstream supply chain that is able to make space components.Ahmed adds that Pixxel started with about 45 percent indigenous content because Isro had qualified local vendors for chips, radios, antennas and GPS receivers.Testing facilities are another area of cooperation. Bellatrix uses Isro’s facilities to fill propellant and validate its data, and Ganapathy says access that once took anywhere from two days to seven months now follows a streamlined process through IN-SPACe. Singh adds that technology transfer lets a startup avoid 5-8 years of R&D on components already proven in space.Capacity, however, is a limit. Ahmed says Isro’s laboratories offer slots when they are free of its own satellite tests, and Pixxel is building its own facility to reduce that dependence. “They had to come up with a framework where we would pay a certain rent per day, and so, the taxpayer money is not being utilised for free by the private sector,” he adds.Pixxel was among the first private companies to use Isro’s laboratories, testing satellite hardware at the UR Rao Satellite Centre in early 2022. Ahmed says there was no established process at the time. “It had never been done before.” Now, he says, IN-SPACe has become the single window for booking Isro’s test facilities, and access has become far easier.Also Read: How India has learnt to build the impossibleWhat’s nextSeveral founders see the division of labour between startups and Isro in terms of capital and risk. Srinath Ravichandran, CEO of Chennai-based Agnikul, says private companies cannot undertake high-end technological projects, like building a space station or developing a human space flight mission, because there is “no business model for that today” and because projects such as these are of “extreme national security importance”. He adds that industry can take over once a technology can become a business. “Isro will open the gates, and then the private sector can come in and make it commercial.”Singh of GalaxEye, too, feels privatisation is a faster route for India’s space sector, while Isro continues long-term research that will become important in 20 or 50 years. “Isro should be at the centre of the ecosystem, becoming an engine to give tech to companies like us”, rather than building what private firms already build, he says.Contractual deals between Isro and the private sector are undertaken through Technology Transfer Agreements (TTAs) and Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) and involve a transfer of technology fee and some licensing cost. So far, IN-SPACe has facilitated 118 technology transfer agreements.Even as access has become smoother for startups, the expanding private role has unsettled some among Isro’s internal ranks. Even as the startups describe Isro as the source of technology, testing and supply-chain capability they depend on, the space agency’s employees are waiting to see what its new role will be.“India’s Space Policy 2023 lays out a clear roadmap for how each stakeholder’s role in the ecosystem will evolve. We will have to wait and watch as the policy is implemented and realises its full potential,” says IN-SPACe chairman Goenka.

Gurpeet Singh spent almost eight years in the navigation group at the UR Rao Satellite Centre in Bengaluru, the lead centre for the design, development, and realisation of all satellites within Isro and where most of India’s satellites are built.
But he left in July 2025 to join Newton School of Technology as an associate director of academics, and also advises Vyomic, a space startup working on low-Earth-orbit navigation.
He believes people often quit Isro because they feel “that mundane, repetitive work is happening at Isro and don’t want to associate with that,” he says.

People expect “specialised R&D inside Isro, which is the usual assumption”, he says, adding that, as Isro transfers repetitive tasks, such as end-to-end satellite fabrication, to private companies, that should give its scientists room for deeper research and riskier missions.
The second reason, he says, is opportunity in the private sector, which has grown.
The third reason is that a number of scientists leave to pursue higher education.
“[But] that was always there.
That is not a new phenomenon,” he says.
Despite the exits, however, he adds that Isro’s size gives it resilience.
“It’s such a large organisation, there is huge inertia,” he says.
“If one or two people leave, overall momentum is not much affected.” Hiring is still open and young engineers still want to join, he says, and the gap is “manageable”.
Bharatiya Antariksh Station is Isro’s planned five-module space station, with the first module due by 2028 and completion by 2035The support ISRO provides.
It is not just engineers who want continued association with Isro.
Founders, too, describe continuing reliance on Isro’s infrastructure and supply chain.
Suyash Singh, CEO of GalaxEye, says Isro’s decades of in-house building has left India with a downstream supply chain that is able to make space components.
Testing facilities are another area of cooperation.

Bellatrix uses Isro’s facilities to fill propellant and validate its data, and Ganapathy says access that once took anywhere from two days to seven months now follows a streamlined process through IN-SPACe.
Singh adds that technology transfer lets a startup avoid 5-8 years of R&D on components already proven in space.
Capacity, however, is a limit.
Ahmed says Isro’s laboratories offer slots when they are free of its own satellite tests, and Pixxel is building its own facility to reduce that dependence.
“They had to come up with a framework where we would pay a certain rent per day, and so, the taxpayer money is not being utilised for free by the private sector,” he adds.
Pixxel was among the first private companies to use Isro’s laboratories, testing satellite hardware at the UR Rao Satellite Centre in early 2022.
Ahmed says there was no established process at the time.
“It had never been done before.” Now, he says, IN-SPACe has become the single window for booking Isro’s test facilities, and access has become far easier.
What’s next.
Several founders see the division of labour between startups and Isro in terms of capital and risk.

Srinath Ravichandran, CEO of Chennai-based Agnikul, says private companies cannot undertake high-end technological projects, like building a space station or developing a human space flight mission, because there is “no business model for that today” and because projects such as these are of “extreme national security importance”.
He adds that industry can take over once a technology can become a business.

“Isro will open the gates, and then the private sector can come in and make it commercial.” Singh of GalaxEye, too, feels privatisation is a faster route for India’s space sector, while Isro continues long-term research that will become important in 20 or 50 years.
“Isro should be at the centre of the ecosystem, becoming an engine to give tech to companies like us”, rather than building what private firms already build, he says.

Contractual deals between Isro and the private sector are undertaken through Technology Transfer Agreements (TTAs) and Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) and involve a transfer of technology fee and some licensing cost.
So far, IN-SPACe has facilitated 118 technology transfer agreements.
Even as access has become smoother for startups, the expanding private role has unsettled some among Isro’s internal ranks.
Even as the startups describe Isro as the source of technology, testing and supply-chain capability they depend on, the space agency’s employees are waiting to see what its new role will be.
“India’s Space Policy 2023 lays out a clear roadmap for how each stakeholder’s role in the ecosystem will evolve.
We will have to wait and watch as the policy is implemented and realises its full potential,” says IN-SPACe chairman Goenka.

stories.title: Tata Comm to invest $450M in high-speed fibre network to connect AI data centres
stories.summary: The first phase of the programme will focus on the Mumbai-Pune-Hyderabad-Chennai corridor, one of India's most important Al and hyperscale growth routes.

article_sentences: The first phase of the programme will focus on the Mumbai-Pune-Hyderabad-Chennai corridor, one of India's most important Al and hyperscale growth routes.
Tata Communications on Monday said it plans to invest $450 million (about Rs 4,280 crore) for setting up a high-speed long-haul fibre network in India to connect AI data centres.

Subsequent phases will expand connectivity into emerging East Coast and Western India data centre ecosystems, including Vizag, Bhubaneswar, Jamnagar, GIFT City and other strategic locations, the company said in a statement.

"Tata Communications...announced strategic investments of close to USD 450 million to build an Al super highway in India - a high-speed, low-latency network fabric connecting India's key Al data-centre corridors.
The company will build around 10,000 kilometers of the new long-haul fibre across India, creating one of the country's largest Al-ready connectivity networks," it said.

Integrated with Tata Communications' global network backbone, the Al network aims to provide customers with a seamless, end-to-end connectivity fabric, supporting the performance, resilience and scale required for next-generation Al workloads.
"We are excited about the opportunity in the India data centre-to-data centre connectivity, which we believe could evolve into a market exceeding USD 1 billion over the medium term.
With our planned investments, we are building on our existing strengths to create one of the most comprehensive data centre connectivity platforms in the market.
As we scale, a growing proportion of our expansion is being driven by anchor customer commitments and contracted demand," MD and CEO Ganesh Lakshminarayanan said.
Tata Communications said it will enable seamless connectivity between India and major global Al hubs across, positioning India as a strategic gateway in the global digital infrastructure landscape.

In parallel, the company will continue to cater to the requirement of existing enterprise and data centre connectivity requirements by scaling its current national long distance and metro network footprint.
Tata Communications operates one of the largest wholly-owned subsea fibre networks spanning over 5 lakh kilometer of subsea optical fibre and over 2 lakh km of terrestrial fibre.

stories.headline: SC asks states, UTs to allocate funds to build bar rooms, washrooms for women advocates
stories.title: SC asks states, UTs to allocate funds to build bar rooms, washrooms for women advocates
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 26: The Supreme Court on Monday directed all states and Union Territories to allocate funds to build bar rooms, washrooms and other basic amenities for women advocates in district and taluk courts. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana disapproved of the lack of ladies' bar rooms and said facilities should be provided to women advocates regardless of their numbers. "If there are no ladies' bar rooms, we strongly disapprove of it. It is the duty of all high courts and state governments to ensure that wherever women members are practising, they are provided an exclusive women's bar room with all facilities. This is the mandate. We do not want to deviate from that. It has to be complied with, whether additional funds or land are required. Whatever is required must be done," the bench said, posting the matter for hearing on December 2. The top court was hearing a plea filed by a group of women advocates concerning the accessibility, inclusiveness and long-term sustainability of women lawyers in the legal profession. Earlier, the court had stressed the need to create conditions that enable women advocates to discharge their professional responsibilities effectively, safely and on equal terms. Taking note of issues raised in a plea that flagged the absence of adequately equipped ladies' bar rooms and other essential facilities in most courts, tribunals and commissions across the country, the apex court had said the concerns raised could not be brushed aside as a matter of mere convenience.
